key_insight: Training robots on pairwise human preferences over executions (rather than hand-designed rewards) lets them learn fine-grained, subjective manipulation skills (e.g., peeling with a knife) that align with human notions of quality.
problem_solved: Enables learning and evaluation of contact-rich, force-sensitive tasks whose success is continuous and subjective—where explicit reward engineering is impractical.
method: Collect human preference labels over short execution clips or outcomes (pairwise comparisons or ratings).
Train a learned reward model that predicts human preference scores from sensor/trajectory data.
Optimize a contact-aware manipulation policy (via RL/IL/finetuning) using the learned reward to produce high-quality, human-aligned behavior.
impact: Reduces the need for brittle, task-specific reward engineering and provides a scalable way to teach robots subtle, subjective skills—opening practical progress on food prep, surgery-adjacent tasks, and craftsmanship.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: human pairwise comparisons → learned reward model → policy optimization → robot executing peeling
Before/after photo pair or sequence showing low- vs high-quality peel with human preference annotations
Chart plotting learned reward score vs. human preference/agreement (correlation/ROC)
Icon set: knife/peeler, human thumbs up/down, force/contact sensor, RL/brain symbol
paper_title: How to Peel with a Knife: Aligning Fine-Grained Manipulation with Human Preference
paper_authors: Toru Lin, Shuying Deng, Zhao-Heng Yin, Pieter Abbeel, Jitendra Malik
